newsitem.title: JORDAN: Opposition says Jordan begging Israeli forgiveness.
newsitem.headline: Opposition says Jordan begging Israeli forgiveness.

text.p: Jordanian opposition leaders on Saturday criticised their government for "begging forgiveness" from Israel for the killing of seven schoolgirls this month by a Jordanian soldier.

Leading Islamist and political opponents of the government calling themselves the Popular Committee for the Defence of Soldier Ahmed al-Daqamsa, who opened fire on the schoolgirls on March 13, accused Jordan of bowing to Israel after the attack.

"We criticise very strongly the way our government begged forgiveness as if we were the terrorists, as if our people are not subject to terrorism daily," committee member Laith Shubailat told a news conference.

"The Israeli government never apologises. On the contrary those who kill Arabs have never been condemned for more than a few years (in jail)," Shubailat, head of Jordan's Islamist dominated Engineers, said.
Jordanian officials swiftly condemned the shooting as an isolated criminal attack and vowed speedy justice.

King Hussein said the killing was a shame on all Jordanians and flew to Israel to pay condolences to the victims' families. He later rebuked Daqamsa's army colleagues for not shooting him dead on the spot when he opened fire.
Shubailat, without naming the king, said such comments were "something no civilised society has heard before".

"We condemn the straight orders from the authorities that this man should have been killed and that those who did not kill him were cowards," he said, adding the committee feared for Daqamsa's safety in detention.
"We are very much afraid that anyone would interpret this as a message to go ahead and kill the man," he said.
A lawyer who met Daqamsa last week said he harboured strong anti-Israeli feelings but opened fire on the girls impulsively because he said they mocked him while he was praying.
The eight-man committee includes Shubailat, Islamist parliamentarian Hammam Said, former Prime Minister Ahmed Obeidat and prominent lawyers.

Former parliamentarian Riyadh al-Nawaysa said security forces tried repeatedly to prevent a small group of committee members from reaching Daqamsa's family in the northern village of Ibdr on Saturday. When they reached the family home security forces broke in, he said.
"There is a blockade around the town and around the family," he told the news conference.
Shubailat said they wanted to give Daqamsa's relatives money but feared it would be taken from the family by officials.
Daqamsa's attack followed a tough warning from King Hussein that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing the Middle East towards "an abyss of bloodshed".
Many Jordanians were shocked by the shooting, but not all shared King Hussein's public grief.
"The girls were victims and Daqamsa was a victim too," Islamic Action Front spokesman Hamza Mansour said. "But the real criminal was Netanyahu."
